From threats to inviting us to tea: SJP changes its tune (and fees)
Ali Hussain meets the wealth manager’s chief executive to ask him about how the company is overhauling its charges after intense criticism/
THE SUNDAY TIMES
The decision by SJP, a FTSE 100 company that manages £190 billion for almost a million customers, came as the City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), tightened its grip by introducing new consumer duty rules demanding “good outcomes” for clients. It also marked a significant victory for The Sunday Times after years of warning about the firm’s charges.
FitzPatrick, affable and earnest, readily acknowledges the past missteps. “If you got those things addressed, the opportunity was huge,” he said, hinting at the potential unlocked by a more transparent approach.
The price of change
The most striking change in SJP’s new fee regime is the abolition of the charge of up to 6 per cent on early pension withdrawals.
Since 2017, pension exit charges have been capped at 1 per cent by the regulator, yet SJP had sidestepped this by branding its fee as an “early withdrawal charge”. That linguistic acrobatics act is now being consigned to the history books.
To mitigate some of the inevitable revenue loss, the company is introducing a charge of up to 3 per cent for initial pension advice — there had previously been no charge — and will increase its annual advice fees from 0.5 per cent to 0.8 per cent.
Money newsletter
The latest personal finance and investment news from our money team.
For the first time, SJP will break down the cost of the underlying managed fund, the investment platform and the advice itself, rather than providing just one overall figure. This will finally allow clients to compare SJP with rivals.
So when will the changes take effect? While a leaked presentation to SJP advisers suggested that the changes would be in place by May 27, as reported by Money last month, the official line has since softened to “the summer”.
“The IT wasn’t ready,” FitzPatrick said, adding: “We’re saying that we’re going to do it by the end of the summer. So, when does summer end? The end of August. So it’ll be done by then.”
A month before the new fee structure takes effect, clients will receive two cost illustrations, allowing them to compare both systems. “I don’t want any client to feel that ‘had I known this, I would have waited’. It needs to be transparent,” FitzPatrick said.
Addressing historical wrongs
Last year SJP pledged £426 million to compensate clients who had paid for annual reviews that never materialised. For years, this paper has highlighted the frustration of clients unable to reach their adviser, who is known as a “partner”.
“We didn’t have a system that sat over the whole partnership or have a line of sight at the centre of all the interactions our partners were having with clients,” FitzPatrick said.
A Sunday Times story from earlier this year about the wait for compensation from SJP
THE SUNDAY TIMES
SJP had relied on “spot checks” of a sample of its advisers, but under its new system the company will have oversight of all its partners’ records. This will help the firm’s compliance team to proactively identify concerns. “We can see what [partners] are doing; when last they had engagement with clients. We send them reminder emails to say, some of your clients haven’t seen you for ten months, you should make sure you’ve got an appointment in the diary.”
And what happens if a partner doesn’t play by the new rules? “We said to the partnership, it’s really important that you actually record things properly. So if you don’t record things in the system, you’re not going to get paid,” FitzPatrick said.
And despite the past issues, most clients still value advice. Only 2 per cent, or approximately 20,000 clients, have opted out of annual portfolio reviews — a right that advised investors have had since 2012.
While many clients may not need or want yearly reviews, FitzPatrick said they appreciate the assurance of having an adviser available when needed. “I don’t need to see my adviser every year, but I want to know they are there. I’m very happy to pay a fee, but don’t want my adviser hassling me to see me because I’m comfortable with where I’m at,” he said, paraphrasing a common client sentiment.
The company results certainly demonstrate continued support from clients. Total new investment with SJP increased from £3.97 billion in the first three months of 2024 to £5.14 billion in the same period this year.
• How to invest £50,000
What about performance?
SJP’s latest value assessment report, which all fund managers are required to produce to justify their fees, found that of the 45 funds analysed, 32 provided value overall, including customer service. However, when analysed just for performance only four funds delivered value. Two were too new to be assessed.
FitzPatrick said the reporting of its fund performance is sometimes misleading because it includes all fees, including advice, making direct comparisons with other funds difficult. The new fee structure will allow for a more “apples and apples” comparison and should show SJP’s fund performance in a much better position relative to its peers.
When I asked if advice delivers value for money, FitzPatrick said: “Investment returns are very important. That being said, the story of advice doesn’t begin and end at investment.” For example, excellent investment returns can be eroded by poor tax planning or ill-timed retirement, he said.
“[But] when investment returns are poor we should own up to that and demonstrate what we’re doing to deal with that.”
And what of the infamous cruises and cufflinks, once awarded to SJP’s top product sellers? The lavish incentives are no more, FitzPatrick said. Instead, successful partners now attend “team-building events” that allow them to “connect with and learn from peers, where they can have fun and improve their business”.
The “rip-off” charges that made headlines are being systematically dismantled, replaced by a structure that, on paper at least, promises greater transparency and fairness.

UK wealth manager SJP seeks to draw a line under its past troubles
Britain’s biggest wealth manager to introduce sweeping new fees next month to rebuild its reputation
As the UK’s largest wealth manager St James’s Place makes the final preparations for its new customer charges, the business looks to draw a line under its past troubles.
Sweeping new fees next month seek to rebuild the group’s reputation, which has been savaged by complaints about poor service and opaque charges.
Mark FitzPatrick, who was parachuted in as chief executive at the end of 2023 to turn the group round, told the FT that the clearer charges should help customers “compare and contrast” their products with competitors.
The new model includes separating charges from a “bundled” cost so that customers can more clearly see individual fees for product wrappers, funds and advice.
The move follows regulatory scrutiny over the company’s complicated charging structure, which coincided with a drive by FitzPatrick to clean up its culture after years of excessive perks for top-selling advisers, ranging from overseas cruises to luxury Montblanc pens.
It has also set aside £426mn potentially to repay clients who claimed they received insufficient levels of advice.
But some analysts and consumer champions question whether the clearer charging structure will help the group attract new customers and boost business over the longer term.
“The all-in pricing of St James’s Place has never actually been that different from peers, but its bundled nature made it look more expensive,” said Rae Maile, analyst at Panmure Liberum.
“That meant advisers would spend half of a meeting with a prospective client having to explain how charging worked and how it was comparable really. That time is not now going to be wasted on charging and can be spent on providing clients with the advice that they need.”
It has certainly been a tumultuous period for the Gloucestershire-based company, which boasts the biggest advisory network in the UK with 5,000 financial advisers, nearly a fifth of the total in the country, serving more than 1mn customers managing nearly £190bn of their assets.
Its new fees come in response to Consumer Duty, a sweeping regulation introduced by UK regulator the Financial Conduct Authority, which aims to at ensure customers receive a fair deal from financial services companies.
SJP also suffered from a surge in customer complaints from the beginning of 2023 over the regular advice they should have received, driven by claims management companies.
The wealth manager tweaked its fees when the rules came into force in July 2023, but pressure from financial regulators led it to announce a bigger overhaul later that year, with the changes due to take effect from the end of August.
The group’s new model includes the removal of its controversial “exit” fee or early withdrawal charge, which was applied to investment bonds and pensions. These charges were as much as 6 per cent of investment value and were applied if customers withdrew their money within the first six years.
But some experts question how SJP has managed to charge an exit penalty for customers since Consumer Duty came into force two years ago.
“SJP appear to be addressing the opacity of their fees that has managed to inexplicably escape regulatory requirements that other firms have had to comply with,” said Gina Miller, co-founder of investment firm SCM Direct and a campaigner for clearer industry fees.
SJP’s new fee model has already suffered teething problems, having originally been slated for May. People close to the situation said the delay was due to testing IT systems internally before enacting the changes.
Critics including Miller argue that the delay has potentially allowed its financial advisers to charge higher fees for longer. SJP would charge up to 4.5 per cent as an initial advice fee, although this will be tiered to between 1-3 per cent depending on the amount of money invested once the changes are implemented.
FitzPatrick denied that the firm was trying to “squeeze” clients, noting “that’s not who we are. It’s about making sure a large IT change is done carefully and successfully and with minimum bumps down the road for clients and [the] partnership”.
So what impact will the fee changes have on the business? David McCann, analyst at Deutsche Numis, said the new charges “remain about industry average”, noting that the new structure is “unlikely to materially change the outlook” for SJP’s growth prospects, providing some reprieve for shareholders.
In some cases, fees will be lower for customers. For example, the initial product charge for Isas and unit trusts will drop from 0.5 per cent to zero and the annual ongoing charge will fall from 1.64 per cent to 1.59 per cent. Initial financial advice charges of up to 4.5 per cent will drop to between 1-3 per cent based on portfolio size.
However, some costs will increase. The new ongoing pension and investment bond charge of 1.66 per cent is an increase on the current 0.92 per cent fee for the first six years, but compares favourably over the long term, down from 1.92 per cent in years seven to 10 and from 1.77 per cent after that.
McCann said SJP’s new charging structure will mean a typical client will pay total annual costs of about 1.9 per cent, compared with a range of 1.6-2.1 per cent charged by SJP’s closest rivals.
FitzPatrick is keen to look beyond the summer and the other developments that are in store for SJP’s customers.
One of his focal points is the SJP Financial Adviser Academy, which trains prospective advisers.
“We continue to be a huge source of financial advisers for the market. Over the last five years, SJP has trained 50 per cent of people who have joined the profession,” FitzPatrick says.
“We will continue to invest heavily in the academy to bring new young advisers into the profession, training them up, giving them the skills, because what we want is young clients to have the choice to engage with young advisers their age.”
He said SJP will also continue to develop its use of artificial intelligence to assist both advisers and customers. “We continue to roll out AI across many aspects, not just client-facing, but also how we provide support to advisers.”
Last year, the wealth manager started using artificial intelligence in its call centre to identify any kind of intonation or language used by a client that could suggest that they are a “vulnerable” customer.
FitzPatrick said at the time that the company was using technology “intensively” and that its “big focus” is to “facilitate the productivity and effectiveness of our advisers”.
The chief executive continues to work on SJP’s culture, having axed its notorious annual London gathering at the O2 Arena this year.
In the past, such gatherings were often fuelled with alcohol with top-performing advisers raucously cheered on stage, glamorising its sales culture. Celebrities ranging from former US prime minister Bill Clinton to footballer David Beckham also spoke at the event.
Instead, FitzPatrick said advisers around the country had convened at a series of gatherings, noting that it was still important to ensure that advisers meet and network.
As the group makes the final touches to internal systems for the new charging structure, FitzPatrick will be hoping that the clearer fee model will prove attractive to the next generation of potential customers.

SJP to implement new charging structure next month
St James’s Place (SJP) has confirmed that its new simplified charges will be introduced in August.
The wealth manager believes that separating out advice, product and fund charges will make it simpler for clients to understand and easier for them to compare.
SJP first announced it would be scrapping its controversial exit charges in October 2023.
The move appeared to have been prompted by the Financial Conduct Authority’s increased focus on fair value for customers as part of its Consumer Duty work.
SJP originally held firm with its charging structure when the FCA first revealed its proposals.
But having come under increased scrutiny in the months that followed, the firm had a change of heart.
The new charging structure, which will be implemented from 26 August, means the early withdrawal charge – or exit fee – will no longer apply for new investments.
James Rainbow, chief executive officer at St James’s Place Wealth Management, said: “We see the real value in the relationship between our clients and their advisers every day.
“These changes will make it much simpler to see just how competitive we are on a like-for-like basis for the fully personalised, trusted advice our advisers provide.
“It’s a good thing for our advisers, our business and most importantly our clients, the majority of which will benefit from lower overall charges over their relationship with us.”
As part of these changes, SJP is introducing tiering of initial advice charges (IAC) based on the amount being invested.
Initial advice charges will be tiered at 3% for the first £250,000, 2% for the next £250,000 and 1% on amounts over £500,000. These rates will apply in the majority of cases.
SJP’s ongoing advice charge will be 0.8% per year as charges are realigned to more accurately reflect where clients get the most value.
Its ongoing product charges will be tiered based on the amount invested across a client’s overall portfolio.
For investment bonds and pensions, this tiering will start at 0.35% per annum on the first £500,000 invested, while on Isas and unit trusts the starting point will be 0.27%.
Rainbow added: “Moving to our new charging structure is a major exercise, and we’re now in the final stages of implementation.
“This has required an extensive IT infrastructure build to deliver these changes, with a comprehensive testing plan.
“Alongside this, we have equipped our advisers with a suite of tools and materials so they continue to deliver the best possible outcomes to clients as we implement these changes.”
In addition, SJP has looked at the costs associated with running each individual fund.
SJP’s group investment director Tom Beal said: “We have spent years building our range, using our reach and size to create economies of scale, negotiating competitive terms for our clients while selecting the best managers from around the world.
“This will now be more visible to our clients and more readily comparable to our peers when it comes to performance, which up until now included the cost of advice and the product wrapper.
“This weighed on our comparative performance against peers who keep such costs separate.
“Our new structure will enable clearer performance comparisons, making it easier for clients to see value.”
SJP has started communicating the changes to clients.
Existing clients will transition to the new ongoing advice and product charges either on 26 August or once they come to the end of their early withdrawal charge period for bonds and pensions.

What SJP’s new fees will mean for customers — and their money
The wealth manager’s shake-up begins in August after criticism of its complicated and often expensive charges
After criticism of its charging structure, St James’s Place (SJP) said in October 2023 that it planned to reduce fees and make them more transparent, then later told staff that it would implement the changes in May this year. But the plans were postponed after pushback from its advisers, who said that there wasn’t enough time to adapt their systems.
The decision to overhaul the charging structure came after the City watchdog, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), brought in new consumer duty rules which demand “good outcomes” for clients.

SJP is changing its initial advice fee of 4.5 per cent to a tiered structure: the first £250,000 will cost 3 per cent, the next £250,000 will have a fee of 2 per cent and anything over £500,000 will be 1 per cent.
For example, if you had £400,000 you would pay 3 per cent on the first £250,000 (£7,500) and 2 per cent on the next £150,000 (£3,000). You would pay a total of £10,500 for the initial advice, which works out at 2.63 per cent.
The firm’s ongoing advice fee of 0.5 per cent — which typically pays for a yearly review — is increasing to 0.8 per cent. This is roughly in line with the rest of the industry, but will make things more expensive for loyal customers who will not benefit from the reduced cost of initial advice.
SJP customers will also pay an ongoing product charge for their investments. Bonds and pensions cost 0.35 per cent a year, decreasing gradually for larger sums down to 0.25 per cent for any money over £3 million. Isas and unit trusts cost 0.27 per cent, decreasing gradually to 0.17 per cent on amounts over £3 million.
The charges for fund management have also been reviewed. The amount charged varies but SJP said it ranges from 0.09-0.69 per cent for 95 per cent of its funds.
As part of the overhaul, SJP has split its charges into three components: the advice charge, the product charge and the fund charge. While this makes it easier for new customers to work out what they are paying for, it means that comparing the new fees to the old system is complicated. Part of the controversy around SJP’s old fees was their lack of transparency.

SJP said that a very small group of customers may end up paying more due to the prices of certain funds increasing during the restructure.
The company said that moving to the new charging structure had required an “extensive IT infrastructure build”. These changes will make it much simpler to see just how competitive we are on a like-for-like basis for the fully personalised, trusted advice our advisers provide.
“It’s a good thing for our advisers, our business and most importantly our clients, the majority of which will benefit from lower overall charges over their relationship with us.”

St James’s Place finally scraps exit charges – is it time to move your money out?
Britain’s biggest wealth manager overhauls complex fee structure after years of client complaints
Charlotte Gifford
St James’s Place will introduce its much-anticipated new charging structure next month, reducing costs for some clients, but others will still be subject to its controversial exit charge for six years to come.
Britain’s biggest wealth manager, which has long been criticised for the complexity of its fee model, first announced the overhaul in 2023 following the introduction of new regulations by the City watchdog.
In the same year, The Telegraph revealed that some clients had paid thousands of pounds for advice they did not receive, driving a surge in complaints from claims management firms.
The firm, which looks after the pensions and savings of more than one million clients, came under pressure after the Financial Conduct Authority published new “consumer duty” rules.
It has since earmarked £426m for potential refunds in relation to the scandal.
After a tumultuous few years, the new charging structure – which also does away with the controversial “early withdrawal charge” for new customers – is a chance for the firm to draw a line in the sand.
So, is this the moment to leave St James’s Place for good – or give it another chance?
James Rainbow, chief executive at St James’s Place, said: “I wouldn’t understate the extent of the change we are making. It’s been the result of 18 months of significant work from across the St James’s Place organisation.”
As part of the overhaul, the firm is now separating out its charges into advice fees, product fees and fund fees. Previously, the wealth manager bundled up its charges, making it extremely difficult for clients to work out how much they were paying.
How the new charges work
Some costs are coming down. St James’s Place used to charge an initial advice fee of up to 4.5pc, but now this will now be tiered based on the amount invested.
This means a new client would pay £10,500 upfront on a £400,000 sum, according to the firm’s calculations.
However, the annual advice fee is increasing from 0.5pc to 0.8pc. The firm said this was to reflect “where clients get the most value”.
An annual advice fee of 0.8pc is the industry average, according to research from the Financial Conduct Authority published in 2020.
The firm is also launching tiered product charge. The fees are 0.35pc for investment bonds and pensions, falling gradually depending on the amount invested, with 0.25pc due on sums over £3m.
For Isas and unit trusts, the charge is 0.27pc, dropping to 0.17pc on amounts over £3m.
Until now, the price of a fund has included advice charges. But going forwards, the firm is stripping these out, which should make investment performance easier to compare.
Fund charges will now range between 0.09pc and 0.69pc, with the average at 0.52pc.
Altogether, the ongoing charges for a client with a pension add up to roughly 1.67pc each year.
How St James’s Place compares
Holly Mackay, of research firm Boring Money, said this put St James’s Place “pretty bang on in the middle of the pack”, compared to other wealth managers.
She said: “On average, most St James’s Place clients will be better off. A big problem with their previous charging structure was its complexity – it was head-bangingly difficult to work out what you were paying and then compare [with others].”
Most of its funds are cheaper following the restructure. However, a minority now cost more.
St James’s Place said that the majority of investors would see their charges go down regardless, because clients tend to hold a combination of funds in a portfolio.
But a small number of clients will see their overall fees go up. The firm said it was writing to these clients to inform them.
Pensions and investment bonds will be more expensive in the short-term. The new charges work out at about 1.67pc per year, up from 0.92pc in the first six years under the previous system.
However, they compare favourably over the long-term – down from 1.92pc in years seven to 10, and from 1.77pc after that.
One of the biggest changes has been the removal of the so-called “early withdrawal charge”.
St James’s Place used to levy a charge if a client with pensions or investment bonds left the business within six years. The charge applied on a sliding scale – reducing from 6pc in year one to 1pc in year six. This was designed to recoup initial fees which were spread over six years, the firm argued.
New clients will no longer have to pay this fee if they want to move their money. Investments outside of the six-year window will move into the new charging structure from August.
But those with pensions and investment bonds who joined the firm in the last six years will still face a penalty if they leave within that timeframe. In fact, any money added to pensions or investment bonds in the last six years would be subject to the charge if the client left.
Lee Goggin, of the website Find A Wealth Manager, said: “I would be mightily peeved if, as an existing client, I still had to endure the early withdrawal charge, and yet new clients aren’t caught by this ridiculous fee.”
Mr Goggin also said he thought the fund charges were still “at the upper end” of the market.
“For high-net-worth investors, particularly those with larger portfolios, the total cost of investing with St James’s Place is likely to remain steep when compared to other, more modern discretionary managers or platform-based models offering low-cost passive funds.”
St James’s Place said that nearly 95pc of its funds will now rank below average in terms of cost for the relevant fund sector.
Mr Rainbow said: “We see the real value in the relationship between our clients and their advisers every day.
“These changes will make it much simpler to see just how competitive we are on a like-for-like basis for the fully personalised, trusted advice our advisers provide. It’s a good thing for our advisers, our business and most importantly our clients, the majority of which will benefit from lower overall charges over their relationship with us.”

It’s no longer a rip-off, but I’d still never give my money to St James’s Place
Britain’s biggest wealth manager has finally overhauled its complex fee structure
The two questions I get asked the most, once people realise what I do for a living, are “Do you think I should invest in crypto?” and “Can you recommend any financial advisers?”.
My answer to the first question is, of course, that cryptocurrency is not an investment – but if you fancy a flutter, go for it, or stick a tenner on the horses.
Paying for financial advice is anathema to a financial journalist. Avid readers of The Telegraph are well-armed to tackle the major personal finance questions: how much to save into a pension; what to invest your Isa in; where to find the best mortgage and savings rates; and how to cut your tax bill.
There are some areas where you must, under the City watchdog’s rules, speak to a regulated financial adviser – equity release, transferring a defined benefit pension and so on.
But for other decisions, many people, perhaps the majority, don’t have the time or inclination to work everything out themselves. The more complicated your finances, the more likely you would benefit from some hand-holding.
Tax advice, in particular, can be invaluable, and a good adviser can save a client thousands of pounds quite easily.
Which brings us to St James’s Place, Britain’s biggest wealth manager. It claims to have more than one million customers, and manages a record £190bn. Its target is the “mass affluent”, those with decent pensions and savings, but not the mega-wealthy.
However, for years, it has been dogged by claims that its fees were high and opaque. It also operated a controversial “early withdrawal charge”, which could be as high as 6pc.
In countless articles, it defended this charge, and claimed it wasn’t an exit penalty, but simply a way of recouping fees it would otherwise forgo. St James’s Place also claimed the charges offered “strong client value”, and that customers understood it (which was total nonsense – I could barely get my head around it).
The issue came to a head last year when the wealth manager was forced to set aside £426m for compensation when it discovered some clients had not been receiving annual reviews from their “partners”, the name for its army of self-employed advisers.
Clearly, it needed to change. This week, St James’s Place finally confirmed a new charging model from August 26 that splits out the costs of advice, the product (pensions, bonds, Isas and so on) and fund management.
This should make it far easier to compare St James’s Place with other wealth management firms. The exit charge has been abolished for new customers.
Recommended
It has also lowered its initial fee, the charge applied when you first become a client. Previously, customers paid a whopping 4.5pc of the wealth they were handing over, plus an ongoing charge of 0.5pc.
This has been replaced with a tiered initial fee of 3pc on the first £250,000, 2pc on the next £250,000 and 1pc above £500,000. The ongoing charge has risen to 0.8pc.
St James’s Place says a new client with £400,000 to invest would pay £10,500 as an initial advice fee, plus around £3,000 each year for ongoing financial advice. Product and fund fees are charged on top.
Under the old model, the same £400,000 in a pension would have been charged £18,000 initially (but spread over six years) plus £1,900 ongoing each year.
While the new charges are roughly in line with the rest of the industry, it still feels like a huge chunk of change to be handing over.
And remember, with the kind of percentage fees commonly used by wealth managers and stockbrokers, if your investment grows, you pay more in fees. This is despite the fact that in many cases, your wealth is being inflated by global markets, not the skill of an adviser or fund manager.
St James’s Place is also what is known as a “restricted” adviser, meaning it will only ever recommend certain solutions or investments. A true independent financial adviser can, in theory, recommend anything under the sun.
My financial needs are simple. A stocks and shares Isa filled with passive tracker funds that cost pennies per year, and a company pension where I put in as much as I can afford.
Increasingly, the cost of investing is coming down. Brokers such as Interactive Investor charge fixed fees, which can be incredibly cheap depending on how much you have saved.
But there will always be people who need more help. The Financial Conduct Authority has finally recognised this, and is changing its rules to allow pension and Isa providers to offer basic advice to help people avoid the biggest mistakes. Currently, DIY platforms have been too scared of compensation claims to give so much as a nudge to customers.
If you do want fully-fledged advice or wealth management, make sure you wholly understand what you’re paying for in pounds and pence. Ask how many reviews you will get, and whether you should be in passive funds rather than expensive active ones.
Lastly, haggle on the fees. The more money you have, the harder you can squeeze.

St James’s Place shrinks customer compensation pot and will buy back shares
UK’s biggest wealth manager says inflows doubled in first half as it puts turbulent period behind it
St James’s Place has reduced the amount of money it has set aside to compensate customers who alleged they had received insufficient financial advice, freeing up millions of pounds for share buybacks.
The FTSE 100 group said on Thursday that it has released £63.4mn after tax from a redress pot set up last year as part of a review into whether clients had received the financial advice they were paying for.
The Gloucestershire-based company said this money would be returned to shareholders through a share buyback, after the regulator provided guidance earlier this year giving wealth managers greater clarity on the amount of compensation they might need to provide. In total, the group will buy back £95.5mn of shares, following a separate interim buyback worth £32.1mn.
The buybacks comes as SJP reported a doubling of net inflows to £3.8bn in the first half of the year compared with a year ago, beating analysts’ expectations and boosting its total assets under management to £198.5bn.
Chief executive Mark FitzPatrick said the group was also “on track” to achieve its target of cutting £100mn a year from its cost base by 2027.
The turnaround comes after a challenging period for the wealth manager whose shares plummeted in 2023 when it bowed to pressure from regulators to overhaul its fees to comply with new consumer-focused rules.
Andrew Lowe, analyst at Citi, said that SJP’s net flows were “stronger than expected”, adding that the share buyback from the release of the provision was a “positive surprise” for shareholders.
SJP is now gearing up to implement its new fee structure near the end of August, which will separate various charges so customers have better transparency over the cost of advice, products and other services. The company will also remove its controversial exit charge on certain products.
FitzPatrick added that SJP was preparing to launch a new fund investing in cheap index trackers, as the cost of investments would become more visible to customers under the new charging structure.
Shares in SJP rose 6 per cent in morning trading.

SJP claws back £85m after reviewing ongoing advice compensation
St James’s Place (SJP) has clawed back £85m of the money it expected to pay out to compensate customers for historic ongoing advice charges.
Last year, SJP announced it had set aside £426m for potential client refunds – news that caused its share price to plummet and saw it drop out of the FTSE 100.
However, in its half-year results published today (31 July), the wealth manager confirmed that it had now estimated it to be nearer £320m.
This came after reviewing new industry guidance around ongoing financial advice services, issued by the FCA in February 2025.
The money, which equates to £63.4m after tax, will be returned to shareholders through its buy-back scheme.
SJP said: “Following the FCA’s new industry guidance around ongoing financial advice services, we have revised our redress methodology to better align it with both the new industry guidance and our experience from the project to date.
“This revised redress methodology has led to an £84.5m release in the ongoing service evidence provision.”
In February 2024, the Financial Conduct Authority wrote to 20 of the largest advice firms requesting information about their delivery of ongoing services to clients.
In the letter, it laid out its concerns that some had continued to be charged after advice had been given.
In its results, SJP also confirmed it was on track to introduce its new, simpler charging structure on 26 August.
The total cost of implementing it, SJP confirmed, has been £104.8m (post-tax) so far.
SJP also said it is “progressing” and on track with its plan to save £100m in costs by 2027.
Its results revealed another strong financial performance, with net inflows of £3.8bn – double the £1.9bn recorded in the first half of 2024.
Gross inflows stood at £10.5bn, a £2bn (23%) increase from 2024, while funds under management (FUM) grew to a record £198.5bn.
SJP CEO Mark FitzPatrick said: “I am pleased to report strong operating and financial performance in the first half of 2025.
“During the period our highly qualified, professional advisers helped over one million clients to navigate a complex macroeconomic environment, ensuring clients’ financial plans remain on track for the future.
“The investment team has worked hard developing Polaris Multi-Index, a new range of multi-asset funds, which we hope to launch in late 2025.”

The £664m Continental European and £1.8bn Global Emerging Markets funds, both run by Robeco using systematic approaches, meanwhile cost 0.2% and 0.28% respectively. Robeco’s fee stands at 0.08% and 0.15% on the funds, according to the last prospectus to disclose it, with charges lowering as fund assets rise.
A charge of just 0.19% on the £4.2bn Strategic Managed fund is meanwhile the result of February’s switch of manager from Columbia Threadneedle to Royal London in February. Royal London’s fee was disclosed as 0.05% in the last prospectus to disclose it, and the manager is investing in more passive and index strategies.

How stripping out advice fees has changed SJP's fund performance
St James's Place has long argued its 'all-in' fee meant comparisons between the performance of its funds and those of rivals were unfair. But that has now changed.
For years, St James’s Place (SJP) has argued that comparisons between the performance of its funds and those of rivals are unfair.
In value assessments where its funds have come up short against benchmarks, or in response to critical reports flagging its funds’ underperformance, SJP has repeatedly pointed to the difference between its fees and those of rivals.
But now, with the financial advice giant having ‘unbundled’ its pricing, like-for-like comparisons with rivals can be made.
Previously, SJP’s ‘all-in’ fund charge bundled together advice, platform and fund management fees.
This undermined comparisons with other funds, which do not carry these advice or platform fees, SJP would argue.
The FTSE 100-listed advice business was also at pains to point out in value assessments that these fees created an ‘additional hurdle’ when comparing fund performance to benchmarks.
Alongside the introduction of its new charging structure last month, SJP has published simulated performance data stretching back five years for its funds. To mimic its new fee model, this data strips out the impact of advice and platform charges.
In practice, this has involved discounting a 0.775% charge (0.5% for advice and 0.275% for platform services) each year from performance figures for its funds used by ISA customers.
Over five years, SJP’s funds perform on average 5.6 percentage points better under these simulations, with the biggest difference, of 8.1 percentage points, registered by the best-performing fund over the period, SJP Global Value. A 94.4% return over five years turns into 102.6% once advice and platform charges are removed.
Index benchmarks are tough to beat
SJP’s funds have been struggling to beat their index benchmarks. The advice group’s last value assessment, covering the year to the end of March 2024, flagged performance issues for three-quarters of its funds, up from nearly two-thirds the previous year.
Performance is improving, however, and stripping out advice and platform costs from the figures provides a further boost.
The impact of the fee changes can be seen most clearly in one-year performance figures. Over 12 months to the end of August, 10 of SJP’s 38 funds available to UK investors have outperformed their benchmarks. Strip out the advice and platform service charges, however, and the figure rises to 23 out of 38.
SJP’s four flagship Polaris funds, which have each marginally lagged their benchmarks over the past year, are ahead when these charges are removed.
Among SJP’s top-performing funds over the past year are those which have turned things around after lagging in previous years, such as International Equity, Global Growth and Global Emerging Markets.
SJP has implemented changes to the management of each of the funds over the past five years: switching International Equity to cheaper managers in the form of State Street and adopting a similar low-cost approach for Global Emerging Markets by moving to Robeco. The management of Global Growth was meanwhile rejigged in 2022.
Tom Beal, SJP group investment director, said the improvement in performance across the advice business’ funds over the past year was the result of changes to its investment proposition.
‘It’s predominantly down to the fact we’ve been evolving our approach over the past five years,’ he said, referring to the move first to a multi-manager approach on many of its funds, followed by the centralisation of asset allocation as the Polaris funds have grown.
‘We’ve made quite a lot of changes, and that’s starting to come through in performance.’
Over three and five years, stripping out advice and platform charges does not change SJP’s underperformance versus benchmarks. It does improve the picture, however.
Performance against peers
SJP’s relative performance against peers is significantly stronger than its record against benchmarks. More than three-quarters of its funds with Investment Association (IA) sector benchmarks are ahead of their peers over one year, rising to 87% when advice and platform charges are stripped out.
A majority of its funds are meanwhile ahead of peers over three years, while the same is the case over five years once advice charges are stripped out.
Stronger relative performance against peers than indices is perhaps no surprise given the struggles of active managers to outperform markets over the past five years. Research by investment platform AJ Bell found just a quarter of active funds outperformed passive alternatives over the five years to the end of June.
SJP’s multi-asset index benchmarks have proved particularly hard to beat. The advice giant’s Managed Growth, Strategic Income and Balanced Managed funds are all ahead of the average in their IA mixed asset sectors over five years once advice and platform charges are removed, yet trail their indices.
The advice giant’s multi-asset funds – with the exception of Strategic Income – are also benchmarked against the ARC Private Client Indices, which are based on the performance of discretionary portfolios.
Against that measure, SJP’s performance is emphatic: all of its funds benchmarked against ARC indices beat them over one, three and five years, whether advice and platform charges are included or not.
This includes the Polaris range over one year, the InRetirement range over one and three years, and the Strategic Managed, Managed Growth and Balanced Managed funds, over one, three and five years.
Polaris beats LifeStrategy
Increasingly, the best gauge of SJP’s investment performance comes from its Polaris funds. The giant £74bn fund range invests predominantly in SJP’s funds, alongside some index funds, and is for many clients their means of accessing the advice group’s investment proposition.
While the funds are marginally ahead of their index benchmarks over one year, when advice and platform charges are removed, they lag slightly over the period since their launch in November 2022.
Performance against peers is much more impressive, however. Each of the funds has beaten their average returns of rivals in their respective IA sector benchmarks by a significant margin.
The funds have also topped the returns of their equivalents in the low-cost passive Vanguard LifeStrategy range, their closest multi-asset competitors in size, since their launch.
That’s despite a difficult environment for active fund managers over the period. Beal said asset allocation calls, such as favouring undervalued European, UK and Japanese stocks, and the hedging out of US dollar exposure, had driven some of the performance.

The remarkable redemption of St James’s Place
UK’s largest wealth manager has staged a turnaround and is attempting to attract advisers despite scrapping perks and fees
There was an inevitability to St James’s Place’s ejection from the FTSE 100 last year. Long-standing controversy around opaque customer fees, and a hefty compensation pot to cover potential mis-selling, had weighed on its share price for months.
But the UK’s largest wealth manager staged a sharp turnaround after its ignominious exit, rejoining the blue-chip index six months later, at the end of 2024. Shares in the Gloucestershire-based business are up more than 50 per cent so far in 2025, putting it in the top 10-performing FTSE 100 stocks.
In the past few months, a review from the watchdog has meant SJP has been able to claw back some £63mn of its £426mn redress pot earmarked for customers who had not received sufficient levels of financial advice, freeing up more cash for the company to buy back its own shares.
Meanwhile, assets under management have hit a record £198.5bn as the wealth manager doubled client inflows in the first half of the year. The group has overhauled customer fees, a major undertaking following years of criticism over its opaque charges and “exit” fees for people selling out of their products early.
As chief executive Mark FitzPatrick prepares to unveil the group’s third-quarter earnings next week, the spotlight will be on its ability to attract financial advisers under its new charging structure, which cuts the maximum initial advice fee they can potentially earn. SJP is also aiming to cut £100mn of costs by 2027 and generate savings of £500mn by 2030 — half of which would be reinvested back in the business.
Proponents laud SJP’s new fee structure and turnaround. “Under Fitzpatrick’s leadership they have brought charges back into the pack of comparable peers whilst retaining market leadership in a sector that can only continue to grow,” said Richard Buxton, a former fund manager who personally holds SJP shares.
“There was a dislocation between the share price and the company’s transformation,” said Rae Maile, an analyst at Panmure Liberum.
“The market has reflected on itself and the share price has now rebounded, but the company is still being underestimated. It’s still undervalued we believe, and materially so.” SJP’s shares are currently trading at £13.
The new customer charges, which came into effect at the end of August, split costs into their component parts, including fees for advice, the product — such as a pension — and the investment costs. An “exit” penalty — applied to pension and bond products if a customer sold out within six years — was also removed.
But the new model is not without its challenges. The changes followed sweeping Consumer Duty rules introduced by the Financial Conduct Authority in July 2023, aimed at ensuring customers receive a fair deal. The FCA pushed SJP to overhaul its fees after considering that its initial proposal did not go far enough. The implementation of the new charges was also slightly delayed owing to technology issues.
According to David McCann, analyst at Deutsche Numis, the new fee structure results in a typical annual cost of 1.9 per cent of a customer’s investment, which is slightly less than the 2 per cent under its former model, and compares with the 1.6 per cent to 2.1 per cent range charged by its rivals. However, SJP is rolling out lower-cost funds which will bring this average charge down.
For advisers, though, the chance to earn as much as 4.5 per cent through a so-called initial advice charge, which includes giving a client advice at the outset and a financial plan, has dropped to a maximum of 3 per cent.
One person close to the company warned that this could make it harder for SJP to attract financial advisers to join its “partnership” — a fleet of 5,000 advisers across the country.
FitzPatrick told the Financial Times that he did not believe this would be an issue. “We’re not finding that at all. There’s a lot more that we offer our partners . . . than solely a fee, whether it’s the training . . . the technology, the support.”
He pointed to the group’s “academy”, which trains up advisers, noting that a younger generation was being fostered to provide financial advice.
Some analysts have noted that SJP has stopped updating the market on the number of advisers it has. “The level of granularity might not be there going forward because the narrative is more nuanced and the market will decide if we’re successful or not by the quality of our output,” FitzPatrick said.
The effect of the fee changes on the business means that there will be a dent to profits in the second half of this year and next, but growth will resume from 2027, analysts have estimated. “From 2027 onwards, [profits] grow at about a 20 per cent compound annual growth rate,” said FitzPatrick. “So on a 12-month window it’s going to look like it’s going backwards [but] in 24-48 months we enter a very different world.”
Another key part of Fitzpatrick’s turnaround is SJP’s culture; the firm was criticised in the past for its opulent awards to top-selling advisers, ranging from swanky trips overseas to designer bags.
FitzPatrick has ditched the group’s annual gathering at London’s O2 arena as well as its spring sports break at the luxury Gleneagles hotel in Scotland.
But FitzPatrick is aware of the need to ensure advisers continue to meet to preserve the network and a sense of camaraderie. Under the new charging model, this task might become even more of an imperative to entice new advisers.
“Culture is probably the thing that takes the longest to shift and change and evolve,” said FitzPatrick.
“We are announcing to the partnership over the course of the next couple of months a new event programme for next year, that will have a lot of opportunities through the year for the partnership to get together . . . because it is so important.”
SJP will also launch a lower-cost range of investments next month, to help make the group’s investment offering more competitive as its charges are now more accessible. The new Polaris Multi-Index portfolios will be rated according to their risk and will invest in cheaper index trackers based on SJP’s managers setting the asset allocation, bringing the total charge of these investments to 0.2 per cent a year.
“The new range does offer genuinely competitive fund fees, which should improve outcomes, but once you add advice and platform costs, there are still far cheaper, more transparent options available elsewhere,” said Robin Powell, a consumer champion.
“Had these funds launched three decades ago, SJP clients would be significantly better off today,” he added. “Better late than never, perhaps, but it’s a shame that it ultimately took regulatory pressure to force SJP’s hand.”

SJP's property fund closure lands clients with inflated bond tax bills
The closure of SJP's property fund has led to clients trying to surrender investment bonds being unexpectedly hit with inflated tax bills. I know this because my grandparents were affected.
My grandparents have been clients of St James’s Place (SJP) for as long as I can remember. My granddad had a good relationship with his adviser there and refused to move, dismissing stories in the press and questions from relatives.
Sadly, my granddad was diagnosed with dementia several years ago and he died over Christmas. The adviser he’d stayed loyal to has also now left the firm. What remains is a web of bonds and trusts so complex that SJP’s own advisers have struggled to untangle them.
Trying to encash some of these products has led to a litany of frustrating errors, many of which my mum, who is now dealing with a lot of this admin, has graciously let slide.
But a few weeks ago, a ‘certificate of chargeable event’ arrived in the post stating that a gain of £151,144 had arisen on an investment bond, potentially leading to a sizeable tax bill.
This raised alarm bells. Paperwork shows £197,497 was originally invested in the bond in 2019, and after annual 5% withdrawals, it was worth around £170,000 at the time of attempting to surrender it in full in 2024. This means it had only made an actual gain of £16,360.
My family’s former SJP adviser said that based on what she knew of my nan’s income position, the tax charge should be just over £3,000. So, how could they possibly have made a ‘gain’ of £151,144? It had to be a mistake.
Unfortunately, that figure is correct, but it’s the result of a significant error and the knock-on effects of SJP’s property fund closure. It stands to reason that there could be many more people affected.
The advice and investment bond
In 2019, my grandparents were advised to take a considerable amount of money out of their ISAs and invest it into investment bonds through loan trusts. For this advice, they were charged almost £4,000 in adviser fees.
They were advised to do this for inheritance tax planning. But on reflection, we’re not sure why. My nan was clear with the adviser in the meeting that this money may be needed to pay for care, and she was expecting to need to take it out before she died.
The tax rules around bonds and trusts are notoriously complex, but generally, if you fully surrender an investment bond, you are taxed on your actual gain at your marginal rate of tax.
You can withdraw 5% per year from the bond without triggering a chargeable event, and if you don’t use this allowance in one year, it is added to the next year’s allowance. But if you make a ‘partial withdrawal’ after using up your allowance, you are taxed as income on everything over that amount.
The bond was set up with 1,000 segments - the idea being that you could ‘fully surrender’ several segments at once, and in effect make a partial withdrawal without the tax consequences.
At least, that was the idea in theory. Last year, my family asked SJP to fully surrender the investment bond, acknowledging that this would trigger a tax charge on the gain.
However, after the withdrawal had already been made, SJP admitted that it hadn’t been processed as a full surrender, because every segment held exposure to SJP’s suspended property funds.
This meant it had been processed as a partial withdrawal instead, which has now led to a significantly inflated chargeable gain. Around £5,745 of the bond remains tied up in property funds.
SJP suspended its £1.8bn property funds in October 2023 and announced it was closing the funds the following year.
When my mum asked about the consequences of this last year, an SJP adviser said via email: ‘The admin to SJP have confirmed there is no chargeable gain on the money that was withdrawn.’ This turned out not to be the case.
There are some nuances that could bring my nan’s tax bill down, such as whether top-slicing applies. £30,229 of basic rate income tax is also treated as having been paid.
But regardless, the end result is that the tax owed is higher than it would have been had SJP processed the surrender as instructed. At the time of writing, SJP still hadn’t worked out how much tax is due.
The bigger picture
After putting all of this to SJP, the firm advised my family to raise a formal complaint with the business.
But it stands to reason that mine cannot be the only family affected. SJP has around £40.3bn held in its investment bonds, and presumably a large proportion will have underlying investments in SJP’s suspended property funds.
Indeed, it only took one phone call to another adviser before I found someone else who has experienced this exact situation.
The adviser, who previously worked for SJP and asked not to be named, told me their client inherited several SJP investment bonds and tried to fully encash them in July 2024.
The client was sent a withdrawal statement with an estimated tax charge based on the bond withdrawal being a full surrender.
When the client came to submit her tax return for 2024/25, she contacted SJP to confirm her tax charge.
Only then did she discover her withdrawals had gone through as partial withdrawals, because some of the money was trapped in suspended SJP property funds. The partial withdrawal meant the chargeable gain arose at the end of the bond’s policy year, not the tax year.
As a result, her tax charge is around three times higher than it would have been had the withdrawal been processed as a full surrender. The client, who is an accountant, is adamant she was never told about the property fund issue, or that the partial withdrawal would increase her tax bill.
The adviser told me: ‘There was an absolutely massive failing regarding encashing this bond. This is basic stuff - obviously bonds are complex, but I wouldn’t make this kind of mistake.
‘But there are also questions about why they are putting money into property funds that can be suspended in the first place when it means this could happen.
‘If you require property as part of a portfolio, there are ways to do that without investing in funds that can be suspended. There will definitely have been a lot of people affected by this.’
The adviser said their client works in financial services and is very clever, and yet was completely stumped by what happened here. It took the adviser considerable time to work out what happened. My (financially astute) mum and I spent hours trying to figure out what had gone on.
If all of these people with financial backgrounds struggled to figure this out, what chance do clients stand? Had my nan been the one dealing with this, she may have been confused, but it’s unlikely she would have suspected an error. She would have simply paid the tax.
Greg Moss, an IFA at Eleven.2 Financial Planning, said: ‘This scenario is the stuff of nightmares. I’ve never really thought about the consequences of property funds for investment bonds before. I can see how it could happen - but it shouldn’t happen.
‘I’ve seen these kinds of problems happen with pensions where people can’t transfer their whole pot because some of their money is trapped in a property fund, but in that scenario, there aren’t tax consequences. This error has led to the client actually owing more tax - it’s a serious mess up.
‘The whole thing raises a lot of questions, including why their money was invested in property funds in the first place. I also agree it’s unlikely that this hasn’t happened before. The clients will have to be compensated, or their complaints should be upheld by the FOS.’
SJP’s response
We asked SJP the following questions:
Have other clients been impacted by this and how many?
How is the firm dealing with these situations?
Will SJP compensate clients and pay the inflated tax charge?
How will SJP prevent similar issues arising in future?
What is the point of segmenting bonds if they all hold funds that could be suspended?
A spokesperson said: ‘SJP takes all client concerns very seriously and encourages clients to raise them through our formal complaints process, which allows us to review individual circumstances and any advice provided, including on tax, withdrawals, and suitability.
‘Property investments have historically been used as part of a diversified portfolio because of their potential to provide long-term income and diversification benefits. At the time these investments would have been recommended, property funds were included in our portfolios, and their closure could not reasonably have been foreseen.
‘Investment bonds are structured into multiple segments to provide flexibility and tax efficiency when making withdrawals. Each segment contains a proportional share of all the underlying funds selected. This is standard industry practice and is designed to allow clients to manage withdrawals over time.’

Why have financial advisers lost trust in these British investment houses?
St James’s Place, Aberdeen and Baillie Gifford have topped the table as the fund managers which have lost the most trust among UK financial advisers and discretionary fund managers in 2025.
This is according to study carried out by the FT Commercial Insights team.
The wide-ranging FT Fund Image UK 2025-26 study, shared with FT Adviser, canvassed the opinions of more than 500 financial advisers and advisers with discretionary permissions who read FT Adviser.
Of the respondents, 78 per cent were financial advisers or planners, and 22 per cent were asset allocators or advisers with discretionary permissions.
Among the questions asked was: ‘Which companies do you feel have been the least trustworthy over the course of the past year?’
Based on the responses where respondents ranked fund managers 1, 2, or 3 in terms of loss of trustworthiness, the three least trusted, in order, were:
St James’s Place
Aberdeen
Baillie Gifford
Liontrust came a close fourth to Baillie Gifford. These were all UK fund management houses.
The majority of respondents cited their reasons for loss of confidence as being:
Article continues after advert
Underperformance — 34 per cent
High fees/poor value for money — 17 per cent
Poor client/ adviser service — 14 per cent
By contrast, international giants and vertically integrated companies led the field in terms of ‘Most trustworthy asset manager servicing the UK retail and HNW segment’, with US passive fund giant Vanguard taking the lead.
This was followed closely by Quilter and Rathbones in third place.
Qualities that formed the top reasons why advisers and DFMs had confidence in such companies were:
Transparency and clear communications — 22 per cent
Track record, consistency and performance — 18 per cent
Heritage, brand and scale; Service quality, access and relationships — each at 14 per cent.
When it comes to what advisers felt was a mark trustworthiness, cost only garnered 10 per cent of the votes, indicating that cost is not a primary consideration when it comes to choosing fund managers.
According to the comments, advisers valued “Trusted relationships, proactive communication and real support”.
It should be noted the fielding period of the survey was between May/June 2025, so many of the advisers’ and DFM’s responses will not account for any changes providers have made in the second half of 2025.
With that in mind, the article focuses on the top four asset managers, in whom advisers said they had lost confidence.
1) St James’s Place
Verbatim responses from advisers, when asked why they felt that they had lost faith in the FTSE 100 listed company, included comments relating to charges.
One anonymous adviser, from a firm managing up to £10mn in client assets, commented: “St. James’s Place has faced mounting scrutiny over its charging structures.
“This has resulted in substantial provisions being set aside for client redress, damaging both trust and the firm’s reputation.”
In 2024, SJP announced it would overhaul its fee model after mounting pressure. These changes came into effect in H2 2025.
It is understood SJP has set aside £320mn for potential redress claims.
The adviser added: “These issues, combined with a perceived lack of value in investment performance relative to fees, have raised serious questions about governance, oversight, and long-term client alignment.”
A spokesman for SJP noted the survey was carried out before the changes it made to its charging structure in the second half of the year, or the introduction of its Polaris Multi-Index range.
The spokesperson said: “St. James’s Place operates a vertically integrated Partnership model rather than an IFA platform, meaning respondents to this survey do not use our proposition, systems, or investment approach.
“Following the introduction of our new charging structure to improve transparency and comparability, client trust remains strong, reflected in retention above 95 per cent.

Clients turned to St James’s Place in pre-budget turmoil
Wealth manager pulled in almost £22 billion of new business last year, but had to deal with nerves over what tax measures Rachel Reeves would announce
The country’s biggest wealth manager weathered the turmoil caused by the budget to pull in almost £22 billion of new business last year, cementing its status as the favoured steward of Middle England’s nest eggs.
An update from St James’s Place on Thursday showed the assets overseen by the FTSE 100 company hit a record £220 billion at the end of December, boosted by inflows of client money as well as investment gains enjoyed by its funds.
It attracted a gross £21.9 billion of new money over the year, up 19 per cent on 2024 and resulting in a net inflow of about £6.2 billion once withdrawals are taken into account. The business received a further £23.6 billion lift from investment returns.

Stock market investors responded to the figures by sending its shares up 14p, or 0.9 per cent, to £15.19½ by Thursday’s close.
Mark FitzPatrick, the wealth manager’s chief executive, said it had benefited from clients turning to it for help amid nervousness in the run-up to the government’s budget in the autumn.
Rumours were rife about possible tax-raising measures the chancellor might unveil in the weeks before she set out her plans in late November. This created a headwind for wealth managers, as some clients rushed to pull money from their pensions over fears, which later proved to be unfounded, that Rachel Reeves might cut tax-free pension lump sum withdrawals.
Yet the budget turbulence also boosted demand for the guidance that wealth managers provide.
FitzPatrick said: “The final quarter was marked by protracted speculation in the lead-up to the autumn budget at the end of November and our new business performance reflected clients’ desire for trusted advice amid this period of heightened uncertainty.”
Even so, its figures for the final three months of the year bear the scars of “elevated short-term outflows, as many clients accelerated tax-free cash withdrawals from their pensions”, although FitzPatrick said that trends had normalised by the end of the year. This pensions uncertainty meant net inflows in the fourth quarter shrank to £570 million, from £1.53 billion a year earlier.
The Cirencester-based St James’s Place operates using a network of thousands of self-employed financial advisers and has become the country’s leading wealth manager since it was founded in 1991. However, it has struggled in recent years, attracting criticism for its complicated fees and for the perks it used to hand to its top-performing advisers.
A clampdown on these perks occurred under FitzPatrick’s predecessor Andrew Croft, who was also forced to announce two revamps of the company’s lucrative fees system in response to regulatory pressure, causing the group’s shares to tumble in 2023.
FitzPatrick has since steered a revival of the business, a turnaround that has included refunding clients who were charged for services they had not received in previous years. It was originally braced for a £426 million hit from the affair but disclosed last July that it had pared back the sum it had set aside to compensate customers to £320 million.

I obsessively check my pension — and so should you
The latest personal finance and investment news from our money team.
Pension contributions cannot be made via salary sacrifice if you are on statutory maternity pay because government guidance says that it must be paid to you in full, so cannot be given up in return for higher employer pension contributions. Employers, however, have to continue to pay pension contributions at the same rate as before the leave — covering your contributions, and theirs. In my case this was completely missed.
And I was not the only one. Two of my former colleagues, who were on leave at the same time, had the same issue.
Underpayment of pensions is not just a women’s issue, nor is it something that just affect private schemes. Thousands of pensioners have also been getting a smaller state pensions than they should.
Many pensioners have been underpaid an estimated total of more than £1 billion because of administrative failings within the state pension system. The actual total owed is not expected to be known until March 2027.
• The pension payroll blunder costing families thousands
And while the Department for Work and Pensions will automatically refund many, in some instances you need to apply to get what you are legally owed. Sadly, some were underpaid for decades or even died without ever getting the state pension that was rightfully theirs.
And while receiving too little has been a problem with pensions, paying too much and getting ripped off has been rife in the investment industry.
In 2024, after years of reporting on its practices by this newspaper, the UK’s largest wealth manager, St James’s Place, was forced to put aside £426 millionin compensations for charging for financial advice that customers never had.
The firm had been automatically opting customers into paying for annual financial reviews, charging 0.5 per cent of the value of their investments and pensions. But while some received reviews in the first couple of years, many investors said they then stopped altogether. The payments, however, continued — year after year after year.
A customer with a £1 million pension may have paid £5,000 annually for the non-existent reviews, but may not have realised for years, having a devastating impact on their investments. Ten of thousands of pounds were lost by thousands of diligent savers.
• The six tax ‘dodges’ that could leave you worse off in 2026
The taxman has been getting things wrong too. For years HM Revenue & Customs has been taking more than it should by overcharging taxpayers because they were given the wrong tax codes.
These are all appalling practices, and while there are rules and regulations in place, you simply can’t be careful enough when it comes to your finances. And, while it doesn’t sound fair, the onus is ultimately on you to make sure that you are being paid or charged correctly. No one else will ever care as much about your money as you do.

sentences.sentence: But why now, for a business that, despite some moves to passive and systematic investment approaches, has historically been wedded to active management?
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: For Hamish Gibberd, one of the range’s fund managers, the move was made possible by the success of the original Polaris range, which has raced to £84bn of assets in just three years.
sentences.label: positive

sentences.sentence: ‘We had really got our asset allocation and portfolio construction process into a very robust space,’ he said.
sentences.label: positive

sentences.sentence:
‘What we were also seeing was a partner, adviser and client demand for ways to access that and have a solution at a different cost point.’
The Polaris Multi-Index fund range carries an ongoing charge of 0.2%, compared to charges ranging from 0.45% to 0.55% on the original Polaris range, which invests predominantly in active SJP funds.
sentences.label: positive

sentences.sentence: SJP has negotiated a fee of just 0.0075% with State Street for the running of 14 underlying tracker funds used by Polaris Multi-Index.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The four new fund-of-funds use the same asset allocation as the original range, targeting equity weighting of 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% at each risk level.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The multi-index range’s selling point, Gibberd believes, comes from the active allocation to the passive vehicles within the fund of funds.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: He, alongside chief investment officer Justin Onuekwusi and director of portfolio management Robin Ellis, decides the asset split within the vehicles.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘It’s not a pure passive solution.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: It’s an index-implemented asset allocation solution, which is quite important because there’s a distinction between those,’ he added.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: While SJP may be a latecomer to passives, Gibberd believes its model may actually help when it comes to making successful long-term calls.
sentences.label: positive

sentences.sentence: ‘Making lots of short-term decisions is very hard,’ he said.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence:
‘Our approach is very much looking out over three to five years and trying to find points of quite extreme dislocation in valuation.’
SJP’s vast internal adviser network ‘really gives us an edge as a fund manager in this space’, Gibberd added, because the managers can stick to positions without worrying about flows.

sentences.sentence: This means that they can take ‘potentially contrarian positions’ on a three-to-five-year view.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘Other multi-asset managers might feel compelled to have a shorter-term view,’ Gibberd said.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence:
‘That’s something that seems to be quite distinct.’

The debate over whether active or passive management is the best strategy is a well-trodden path, and not one Gibberd believes they are taking sides on.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘It’s not an active versus passive decision, which is better, which is worse,’ insisted Gibberd, who started his career as an adviser at SJP in 2014, before moving into portfolio management in 2019.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.label: neutral

sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘For example, we think the US is quite richly valued and the rest of the world is relatively cheap...
sentences.label: positive

If that reverts quickly, then we will act in the portfolio.’

The closure of SJP's property fund has led to clients trying to surrender investment bonds being unexpectedly hit with inflated tax bills.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: I know this because my grandparents were affected.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: My grandparents have been clients of St James’s Place (SJP) for as long as I can remember.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: My granddad had a good relationship with his adviser there and refused to move, dismissing stories in the press and questions from relatives.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Sadly, my granddad was diagnosed with dementia several years ago and he died over Christmas.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The adviser he’d stayed loyal to has also now left the firm.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: What remains is a web of bonds and trusts so complex that SJP’s own advisers have struggled to untangle them.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: Trying to encash some of these products has led to a litany of frustrating errors, many of which my mum, who is now dealing with a lot of this admin, has graciously let slide.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: But a few weeks ago, a ‘certificate of chargeable event’ arrived in the post stating that a gain of £151,144 had arisen on an investment bond, potentially leading to a sizeable tax bill.
sentences.label: positive

sentences.sentence: This raised alarm bells.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: Paperwork shows £197,497 was originally invested in the bond in 2019, and after annual 5% withdrawals, it was worth around £170,000 at the time of attempting to surrender it in full in 2024.

sentences.sentence: This means it had only made an actual gain of £16,360.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: My family’s former SJP adviser said that based on what she knew of my nan’s income position, the tax charge should be just over £3,000.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: So, how could they possibly have made a ‘gain’ of £151,144?
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: It had to be a mistake.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Unfortunately, that figure is correct, but it’s the result of a significant error and the knock-on effects of SJP’s property fund closure.

The advice and investment bond
In 2019, my grandparents were advised to take a considerable amount of money out of their ISAs and invest it into investment bonds through loan trusts.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: For this advice, they were charged almost £4,000 in adviser fees.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: They were advised to do this for inheritance tax planning.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: But on reflection, we’re not sure why.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: My nan was clear with the adviser in the meeting that this money may be needed to pay for care, and she was expecting to need to take it out before she died.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The tax rules around bonds and trusts are notoriously complex, but generally, if you fully surrender an investment bond, you are taxed on your actual gain at your marginal rate of tax.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: You can withdraw 5% per year from the bond without triggering a chargeable event, and if you don’t use this allowance in one year, it is added to the next year’s allowance.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: But if you make a ‘partial withdrawal’ after using up your allowance, you are taxed as income on everything over that amount.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The bond was set up with 1,000 segments - the idea being that you could ‘fully surrender’ several segments at once, and in effect make a partial withdrawal without the tax consequences.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: At least, that was the idea in theory.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Last year, my family asked SJP to fully surrender the investment bond, acknowledging that this would trigger a tax charge on the gain.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: However, after the withdrawal had already been made, SJP admitted that it hadn’t been processed as a full surrender, because every segment held exposure to SJP’s suspended property funds.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: This meant it had been processed as a partial withdrawal instead, which has now led to a significantly inflated chargeable gain.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: Around £5,745 of the bond remains tied up in property funds.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: SJP suspended its £1.8bn property funds in October 2023 and announced it was closing the funds the following year.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: When my mum asked about the consequences of this last year, an SJP adviser said via email: ‘The admin to SJP have confirmed there is no chargeable gain on the money that was withdrawn.’ This turned out not to be the case.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: There are some nuances that could bring my nan’s tax bill down, such as whether top-slicing applies.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: £30,229 of basic rate income tax is also treated as having been paid.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: But regardless, the end result is that the tax owed is higher than it would have been had SJP processed the surrender as instructed.
sentences.label: positive

sentences.sentence: At the time of writing, SJP still hadn’t worked out how much tax is due.
sentences.label: neutral
