The bigger picture
After putting all of this to SJP, the firm advised my family to raise a formal complaint with the business.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: But it stands to reason that mine cannot be the only family affected.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: SJP has around £40.3bn held in its investment bonds, and presumably a large proportion will have underlying investments in SJP’s suspended property funds.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Indeed, it only took one phone call to another adviser before I found someone else who has experienced this exact situation.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The adviser, who previously worked for SJP and asked not to be named, told me their client inherited several SJP investment bonds and tried to fully encash them in July 2024.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The client was sent a withdrawal statement with an estimated tax charge based on the bond withdrawal being a full surrender.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: When the client came to submit her tax return for 2024/25, she contacted SJP to confirm her tax charge.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Only then did she discover her withdrawals had gone through as partial withdrawals, because some of the money was trapped in suspended SJP property funds.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: The partial withdrawal meant the chargeable gain arose at the end of the bond’s policy year, not the tax year.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: As a result, her tax charge is around three times higher than it would have been had the withdrawal been processed as a full surrender.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: The client, who is an accountant, is adamant she was never told about the property fund issue, or that the partial withdrawal would increase her tax bill.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: The adviser told me: ‘There was an absolutely massive failing regarding encashing this bond.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: This is basic stuff - obviously bonds are complex, but I wouldn’t make this kind of mistake.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘But there are also questions about why they are putting money into property funds that can be suspended in the first place when it means this could happen.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘If you require property as part of a portfolio, there are ways to do that without investing in funds that can be suspended.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence:
There will definitely have been a lot of people affected by this.’
The adviser said their client works in financial services and is very clever, and yet was completely stumped by what happened here.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: It took the adviser considerable time to work out what happened.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: My (financially astute) mum and I spent hours trying to figure out what had gone on.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: If all of these people with financial backgrounds struggled to figure this out, what chance do clients stand?
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Had my nan been the one dealing with this, she may have been confused, but it’s unlikely she would have suspected an error.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: She would have simply paid the tax.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: Greg Moss, an IFA at Eleven.2 Financial Planning, said: ‘This scenario is the stuff of nightmares.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: I’ve never really thought about the consequences of property funds for investment bonds before.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: I can see how it could happen - but it shouldn’t happen.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: ‘I’ve seen these kinds of problems happen with pensions where people can’t transfer their whole pot because some of their money is trapped in a property fund, but in that scenario, there aren’t tax consequences.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: This error has led to the client actually owing more tax - it’s a serious mess up.
sentences.label: negative

sentences.sentence: ‘The whole thing raises a lot of questions, including why their money was invested in property funds in the first place.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence: I also agree it’s unlikely that this hasn’t happened before.
sentences.label: neutral

sentences.sentence:
The clients will have to be compensated, or their complaints should be upheld by the FOS.’

Have other clients been impacted by this and how many?

sentences.sentence: How is the firm dealing with these situations?
sentences.label: neutral

From threats to inviting us to tea: SJP changes its tune (and fees)
Ali Hussain meets the wealth manager’s chief executive to ask him about how the company is overhauling its charges after intense criticism/
THE SUNDAY TIMES
The decision by SJP, a FTSE 100 company that manages £190 billion for almost a million customers, came as the City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), tightened its grip by introducing new consumer duty rules demanding “good outcomes” for clients.
It also marked a significant victory for The Sunday Times after years of warning about the firm’s charges.
FitzPatrick, affable and earnest, readily acknowledges the past missteps.
“If you got those things addressed, the opportunity was huge,” he said, hinting at the potential unlocked by a more transparent approach.

The price of change
The most striking change in SJP’s new fee regime is the abolition of the charge of up to 6 per cent on early pension withdrawals.
Since 2017, pension exit charges have been capped at 1 per cent by the regulator, yet SJP had sidestepped this by branding its fee as an “early withdrawal charge”.
That linguistic acrobatics act is now being consigned to the history books.

To mitigate some of the inevitable revenue loss, the company is introducing a charge of up to 3 per cent for initial pension advice — there had previously been no charge — and will increase its annual advice fees from 0.5 per cent to 0.8 per cent.
This will finally allow clients to compare SJP with rivals.
So when will the changes take effect?
While a leaked presentation to SJP advisers suggested that the changes would be in place by May 27, as reported by Money last month, the official line has since softened to “the summer”.
“The IT wasn’t ready,” FitzPatrick said, adding: “We’re saying that we’re going to do it by the end of the summer.
So, when does summer end?
The end of August.

So it’ll be done by then.”
A month before the new fee structure takes effect, clients will receive two cost illustrations, allowing them to compare both systems.

Addressing historical wrongs
Last year SJP pledged £426 million to compensate clients who had paid for annual reviews that never materialised.
“We didn’t have a system that sat over the whole partnership or have a line of sight at the centre of all the interactions our partners were having with clients,” FitzPatrick said.

A Sunday Times story from earlier this year about the wait for compensation from SJP
THE SUNDAY TIMES
SJP had relied on “spot checks” of a sample of its advisers, but under its new system the company will have oversight of all its partners’ records.
“We can see what [partners] are doing; when last they had engagement with clients.

We send them reminder emails to say, some of your clients haven’t seen you for ten months, you should make sure you’ve got an appointment in the diary.”
And what happens if a partner doesn’t play by the new rules?
“We said to the partnership, it’s really important that you actually record things properly.
And despite the past issues, most clients still value advice.
Only 2 per cent, or approximately 20,000 clients, have opted out of annual portfolio reviews — a right that advised investors have had since 2012.
“I don’t need to see my adviser every year, but I want to know they are there.
The company results certainly demonstrate continued support from clients.
Total new investment with SJP increased from £3.97 billion in the first three months of 2024 to £5.14 billion in the same period this year.

• How to invest £50,000
What about performance?

SJP’s latest value assessment report, which all fund managers are required to produce to justify their fees, found that of the 45 funds analysed, 32 provided value overall, including customer service.
However, when analysed just for performance only four funds delivered value.
FitzPatrick said the reporting of its fund performance is sometimes misleading because it includes all fees, including advice, making direct comparisons with other funds difficult.
When I asked if advice delivers value for money, FitzPatrick said: “Investment returns are very important.
That being said, the story of advice doesn’t begin and end at investment.” For example, excellent investment returns can be eroded by poor tax planning or ill-timed retirement, he said.

“[But] when investment returns are poor we should own up to that and demonstrate what we’re doing to deal with that.”
And what of the infamous cruises and cufflinks, once awarded to SJP’s top product sellers?
The lavish incentives are no more, FitzPatrick said.
Instead, successful partners now attend “team-building events” that allow them to “connect with and learn from peers, where they can have fun and improve their business”.
The “rip-off” charges that made headlines are being systematically dismantled, replaced by a structure that, on paper at least, promises greater transparency and fairness.

UK wealth manager SJP seeks to draw a line under its past troubles
Britain’s biggest wealth manager to introduce sweeping new fees next month to rebuild its reputation
As the UK’s largest wealth manager St James’s Place makes the final preparations for its new customer charges, the business looks to draw a line under its past troubles.
Sweeping new fees next month seek to rebuild the group’s reputation, which has been savaged by complaints about poor service and opaque charges.

Mark FitzPatrick, who was parachuted in as chief executive at the end of 2023 to turn the group round, told the FT that the clearer charges should help customers “compare and contrast” their products with competitors.
The new model includes separating charges from a “bundled” cost so that customers can more clearly see individual fees for product wrappers, funds and advice.

The move follows regulatory scrutiny over the company’s complicated charging structure, which coincided with a drive by FitzPatrick to clean up its culture after years of excessive perks for top-selling advisers, ranging from overseas cruises to luxury Montblanc pens.
It has also set aside £426mn potentially to repay clients who claimed they received insufficient levels of advice.
But some analysts and consumer champions question whether the clearer charging structure will help the group attract new customers and boost business over the longer term.
“The all-in pricing of St James’s Place has never actually been that different from peers, but its bundled nature made it look more expensive,” said Rae Maile, analyst at Panmure Liberum.
“That meant advisers would spend half of a meeting with a prospective client having to explain how charging worked and how it was comparable really.

That time is not now going to be wasted on charging and can be spent on providing clients with the advice that they need.”
It has certainly been a tumultuous period for the Gloucestershire-based company, which boasts the biggest advisory network in the UK with 5,000 financial advisers, nearly a fifth of the total in the country, serving more than 1mn customers managing nearly £190bn of their assets.
SJP also suffered from a surge in customer complaints from the beginning of 2023 over the regular advice they should have received, driven by claims management companies.
The group’s new model includes the removal of its controversial “exit” fee or early withdrawal charge, which was applied to investment bonds and pensions.
These charges were as much as 6 per cent of investment value and were applied if customers withdrew their money within the first six years.

“SJP appear to be addressing the opacity of their fees that has managed to inexplicably escape regulatory requirements that other firms have had to comply with,” said Gina Miller, co-founder of investment firm SCM Direct and a campaigner for clearer industry fees.
SJP’s new fee model has already suffered teething problems, having originally been slated for May.
People close to the situation said the delay was due to testing IT systems internally before enacting the changes.
Critics including Miller argue that the delay has potentially allowed its financial advisers to charge higher fees for longer.
SJP would charge up to 4.5 per cent as an initial advice fee, although this will be tiered to between 1-3 per cent depending on the amount of money invested once the changes are implemented.
FitzPatrick denied that the firm was trying to “squeeze” clients, noting “that’s not who we are.
So what impact will the fee changes have on the business?
In some cases, fees will be lower for customers.
Initial financial advice charges of up to 4.5 per cent will drop to between 1-3 per cent based on portfolio size.
However, some costs will increase.

The new ongoing pension and investment bond charge of 1.66 per cent is an increase on the current 0.92 per cent fee for the first six years, but compares favourably over the long term, down from 1.92 per cent in years seven to 10 and from 1.77 per cent after that.
McCann said SJP’s new charging structure will mean a typical client will pay total annual costs of about 1.9 per cent, compared with a range of 1.6-2.1 per cent charged by SJP’s closest rivals.
FitzPatrick is keen to look beyond the summer and the other developments that are in store for SJP’s customers.
One of his focal points is the SJP Financial Adviser Academy, which trains prospective advisers.
“We continue to be a huge source of financial advisers for the market.
Over the last five years, SJP has trained 50 per cent of people who have joined the profession,” FitzPatrick says.

“We will continue to invest heavily in the academy to bring new young advisers into the profession, training them up, giving them the skills, because what we want is young clients to have the choice to engage with young advisers their age.”
He said SJP will also continue to develop its use of artificial intelligence to assist both advisers and customers.
FitzPatrick said at the time that the company was using technology “intensively” and that its “big focus” is to “facilitate the productivity and effectiveness of our advisers”.
The chief executive continues to work on SJP’s culture, having axed its notorious annual London gathering at the O2 Arena this year.
In the past, such gatherings were often fuelled with alcohol with top-performing advisers raucously cheered on stage, glamorising its sales culture.
Celebrities ranging from former US prime minister Bill Clinton to footballer David Beckham also spoke at the event.
Instead, FitzPatrick said advisers around the country had convened at a series of gatherings, noting that it was still important to ensure that advisers meet and network.

As the group makes the final touches to internal systems for the new charging structure, FitzPatrick will be hoping that the clearer fee model will prove attractive to the next generation of potential customers.

SJP to implement new charging structure next month
St James’s Place (SJP) has confirmed that its new simplified charges will be introduced in August.
SJP first announced it would be scrapping its controversial exit charges in October 2023.
The move appeared to have been prompted by the Financial Conduct Authority’s increased focus on fair value for customers as part of its Consumer Duty work.
SJP originally held firm with its charging structure when the FCA first revealed its proposals.
But having come under increased scrutiny in the months that followed, the firm had a change of heart.
The new charging structure, which will be implemented from 26 August, means the early withdrawal charge – or exit fee – will no longer apply for new investments.
James Rainbow, chief executive officer at St James’s Place Wealth Management, said: “We see the real value in the relationship between our clients and their advisers every day.
“These changes will make it much simpler to see just how competitive we are on a like-for-like basis for the fully personalised, trusted advice our advisers provide.

“It’s a good thing for our advisers, our business and most importantly our clients, the majority of which will benefit from lower overall charges over their relationship with us.”
As part of these changes, SJP is introducing tiering of initial advice charges (IAC) based on the amount being invested.
Initial advice charges will be tiered at 3% for the first £250,000, 2% for the next £250,000 and 1% on amounts over £500,000.
These rates will apply in the majority of cases.
SJP’s ongoing advice charge will be 0.8% per year as charges are realigned to more accurately reflect where clients get the most value.
For investment bonds and pensions, this tiering will start at 0.35% per annum on the first £500,000 invested, while on Isas and unit trusts the starting point will be 0.27%.
